extracted.intended_audience: journalists (reporters, editors, producers) who cover traumatic events and survivors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for journalists on how to report on trauma and interact with survivors in ways that produce more accurate stories and reduce harm to sources and journalists alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that trauma impacts the brain, memory and ability to vocalize events
rubrics_metrics.description: Trauma results from events that are physically or emotionally harmful or life threatening and have lasting adverse effects; it can significantly affect perception, judgment, memory and a person’s ability to vocalize their story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites SAMHSA and the Dart Center: eyewitnesses to traumatic events are notoriously unreliable; immediately after a tragedy people may literally be unable to tell their story accurately; months later accounts may be more accurate once sources leave 'fight or flight' mode. Implication: do not expect coherent chronological narratives immediately; treat early accounts cautiously and verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: When getting informed consent, err on the side of overexplaining
rubrics_metrics.description: Informed consent for trauma-informed reporting means clearly informing sources about the nature of the story and obtaining consent to use their name and experiences — and doing so with extra clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t assume sources understand terms like 'on the record' or 'on background' — explain identification options clearly. Offer sources the option to review quotes or change their mind about being quoted before publication. Example: the author allowed interviewees to review quoted excerpts to ensure continued consent and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give power to survivors during the interview and storytelling process
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow survivors control over the interview and storytelling — breaking usual newsroom rules when necessary so sources feel safe and respected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible practices include letting sources choose which questions to answer, allowing them to see questions or parts of the story, asking where they would like to begin, and asking what they hope to achieve by telling their story. Warns against minimizing reactions (e.g., 'that doesn’t seem that bad') and against saying 'I understand' or 'I know how you feel.' Includes advising survivors of planned productions (podcast/video/print) and offering them opportunity to participate so they don't feel talked about behind their back.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask appropriate, non-leading, open-ended questions; avoid 'How do you feel?'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the distressing, overused question 'How do you feel?' and prefer open-ended formulations that are less likely to overwhelm or produce incoherent responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended alternatives: 'How are you now?', 'How did you experience that?', or 'What do you think about ...?' Opt for open-ended prompts and let subjects know they are not required to answer. Example recommended phrasing: 'Where would you like to begin?' or 'Would you tell me what you are able to remember about your experience?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow practical interview planning: care before, during and after
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a plan that protects the survivor’s safety and comfort throughout the interview process, including before, during and after contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let survivors pick the interview location, tell them what questions you plan to ask, ask if there are topics to avoid, check during the interview that they are not reliving the event and offer breaks, and at the end thank them and explain how the interview will be used and when to expect publication. For remote interviews, follow guidance on handling sensitive remote interviews (Dart Center/Healey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat interview subjects with dignity and respect (Dart Center interview tips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete behavioral rules for interviewing victims/survivors to reduce harm and build trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dart Center’s five tips included: always treat victims with dignity and respect; clearly identify yourself; never say 'I understand' or 'I know how you feel'; don't overwhelm sources with the hardest questions first; if you receive a harsh reaction, leave contact details and explain survivors can reach out later. Also: approach people with care, make eye contact, take it slowly and don't rush even in chaotic circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trauma-informed terminology and definitions (follow style guides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt consistent, trauma-informed language and definitions when reporting on trauma and survivors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses The Dart Center Style Guide for Trauma-Informed Journalism as its source for defining trauma-related terminology. Implication: consult and follow an established trauma-informed style guide to choose appropriate, non-stigmatizing language and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for and protect journalists’ own mental well-being
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists covering trauma are at risk of stress and vicarious trauma; they should monitor themselves and practice self-care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of warning signs (inability to concentrate, feeling on edge or numb, inability to feel compassion, sleep problems, anger, increased alcohol use). Self-care tips from the Dart Center: know your limits, take breaks, find a colleague who is a good listener, find hobbies/exercise/spend time with family, and seek counseling if overwhelmed. Prevalence estimates cited: 4% to 59% of journalists have PTSD symptoms depending on beats/locations.
